newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russians simulate planned Mir repairs on Earth.
newsitem.headline: Russians simulate planned Mir repairs on Earth.

text.p: The U.S.-Russian crew of the damaged orbiting station Mir were on Wednesday checking space suits they will wear to repair it, while understudies on Earth simulated the risky operation in a huge pool.

Vsevolod Latyshev, a spokesman at Koroloyov mission control near Moscow, said experts had left for the Baikonur cosmodrome in Kazakhstan to oversee the loading of the Progress M-35 cargo craft which will ferry repair equipment to Mir.

Latyshev said U.S. physicist Michael Foale and Russian colleagues Alexander Lazutkin and Vasily Tsibliyev had enjoyed a quiet night in orbit and resumed preparations for the repairs tentatively planned for July 14.
A mission control spokeswoman denied media reports that Mir was facing problems with its oxygen supply.
"Everything is all right and there are no problems with oxygen," she said. "The Elektron system which produced oxygen on board is working fine."
Mir was damaged during a docking manoeuvre a week ago. A Progress crago craft punctured the Spektr scientific module docked to the station and damaged a solar panel providing power.
Mission control on Monday gave the crew instructions for a daring spacewalk inside the station to restore the power supply.
"The team will spend most of the day checking the spacesuits they will need to enter Spektr, which has been sealed off" Latyshev said.

He said a team of understudies at a training centre at Zvyozdny Gorodok (Star City) outside Moscow were rehearsing the repairs on a model of Mir and the modules attached to it in a six-metre-deep (10 feet) pool.
"The understudy team are trying to simulate every situation the cosmonauts might face when they get into Spektr," Latyshev said, adding that the training would continue for several days.
He said many officials and experts had left for Baikonur, which Russia rents from the former Soviet republic of Kazakhstan, to make sure preparations for the launch of the Progress M-35 go smoothly.

The craft will take electric cables, connections and other equipment to Mir. Officials say the launch has been scheduled for 8.11 Moscow time (0411 GMT) on July 5 and the craft should reach Mir two days later.
"The main problem now is to succesfully launch the Progress," Latyshev said.

Mission control said on Tuesday Mir was in a stable condition and the crew had fully recovered from the stress that followed the collision, the latest in a string of mishaps on the ageing station in recent months.
Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin praised the performance of the crew on Tuesday.
"The lads acted like a single team, regardless of whether they were Russian or American. And this is a good example for the future," he told Interfax news agency.
The setbacks in Mir, which has been in space more than a decade, have raised doubts about Russia's space programme.
But Chernomyrdin made clear to Interfax that Russia was commited to the international Alpha station, due to replace Mir in several years' time.
